points: CHEM 267 or FDSC 213: no credit for both.

title: Math or Physical Science
points: 9 credits, 6 at 300+. Only one each of ATOC 519 or CHEM 519, AEMA 305 or MATH 315.

title: Program Description
points: Resources come from the Earth and return as waste. Geology governs both, and economics shapes energy choices and waste treatment. You learn minerals, rocks, soils, waters and their interactions, plus economic theory and policy on resources, waste and warming.

title: Degree Requirements — B.Sc.
points: To graduate, you need both the program's courses and the degree's requirements, including Foundation and structure (p. 1106). Fitting them together is your responsibility, and SOUSA's Degree Planning Guide helps.

title: Suggested First Year (U1) Courses
points: See the Bieler School's Student Handbook.

title: Program Requirements
points: At most 30 credits at the 200 level, and at least 12 at 400+, counting core and required courses. Courses run on both campuses, so check locations.

title: Core: Required Courses (18 credits)
points: Section 001 downtown or 051 at Macdonald.

title: Statistics
points: One statistics course or equivalent. Overlap rules apply: see Arts' Course Overlap.

title: Natural Resources
points: Only one each of ANTH 451 or GEOG 451, BIOL 451 or NRSC 451, ENVB 529 or GEOG 201.

title: Honours Program in Environment
points: For B.Sc. and B.Sc.(Ag.Env.Sc.) Majors, the B.A. Faculty Program and the B.A. & Sc. Interfaculty Program. A 6-credit, two-term supervised research project in your final year, good preparation for graduate school, with no extra time. If you can't finish Honours you can still graduate in the regular program.

title: Program Description
points: For those in the Interfaculty Program. Apply in March of U2 with program GPA 3.3. B or higher in ENVR 495, CGPA 3.0 and program GPA 3.3 at graduation. 21 credits each in Arts and Science with your minor.
54 credits plus 6 Honours credits. Present at an Honours Symposium and submit your report.

title: Degree Requirements — B.A. & Sc. students
points: Part of a B.A. & Sc.; you need both program and degree requirements. SOUSA's Degree Planning Guide helps, and fitting them is your responsibility.

title: Honours Required Courses (6 credits)
points: ENVR 495D1 and D2 over consecutive terms, or N1 and N2 otherwise.

title: Program Description
points: For the B.A. Faculty Program only. Apply in March of U2, seeing the Program Adviser. Enter with a Program GPA of 3.3; earn at least B in ENVR 495D1/D2; graduate with CGPA 3.0 and Program GPA 3.3. Also complete a minor concentration outside the School.
54 credits of core and domain plus 6 of Honours. Present at the Honours Symposium and give your report to the Adviser.

title: Degree Requirements — B.A. students
points: Faculty and program requirements on p. 151; see an OASIS adviser for planning.

title: Honours Required Courses (6 credits)
points: ENVR 495D1 and D2 over consecutive terms, or N1 and N2 otherwise.

title: Program Description
points: For the B.Sc.(Ag.Env.Sc.) Major only. Apply in March of U2. Enter with a Program GPA of 3.3; earn at least B in ENVR 495D1/D2; graduate with CGPA 3.0 and Program GPA 3.3.
60–63 credits of core and domain plus 6 of Honours. Present at the Honours Symposium and give your report to the Adviser.

title: Honours - Required Courses (6 credits)
points: ENVR 495D1/D2 over consecutive terms, or 495N1/N2 over non-consecutive terms.

title: Program Description
points: For the B.Sc.(Ag.Env.Sc.) Major only. Apply in March of U2. Enter with a Program GPA of 3.3; earn at least B in ENVR 495D1/D2; graduate with CGPA 3.0 and Program GPA 3.3.
60–63 credits of core and domain plus 6 of Honours. Present at the Honours Symposium and give your report to the Adviser.

title: Degree Requirements — B.Sc.
points: To graduate, you need both the program's courses and the degree's requirements, including Foundation and structure (p. 1106). Fitting them together is your responsibility, and SOUSA's Degree Planning Guide helps.

title: Honours Required Courses (6 credits)
points: ENVR 495D1 and D2 over consecutive terms, or N1 and N2 otherwise.

title: Joint Honours Component Environment
points: Taken with a second B.A. Joint Honours Component (p. 160): a two-term interdisciplinary final-year research project under supervision.

title: Program Description
points: Combines Honours in any two Arts disciplines. See an adviser in each department about courses and research. Enter at the end of U1 and keep a Program GPA of 3.30 and CGPA of 3.0. Unlike the Faculty Program Honours, no Minor is needed.

title: Degree Requirements — B.A. students
points: Faculty and program requirements on p. 151; see an OASIS adviser for planning.

title: Program Prerequisites or Corequisites
points: 6–8 credits on top of the program, done by the end of U1: 3 of basic science (or CEGEP Biology 00UK, Chemistry 00UL, Physics 00UR) and one more, such as 3 of calculus (or CEGEP 00UN).

title: Honours Research
points: 6 research credits across both components. If your other component requires 0, 3 or 6, take 6, 3 or 0 of ENVR. The same credits can't count twice.
6–12 more credits chosen with the Adviser, at most 3 at 200–300 level.

title: Diploma in Environment
points: Adds undergraduate Environment coursework to a finished degree. 30 credits at McGill, one year full-time. For B.Sc. or B.A. holders in good standing, through whichever of the three faculties fits your background. The Program Advisor approves courses.

title: Program Description
points: Why environmental problems are complex and contested: global climate, socio-economic challenges, geological and biological change, and ethics and culture.

title: Complementary Courses (12 credits)
points: With the Advisor's approval: 3 credits outside your first degree's area (Natural Sciences and Technology after a B.A., Social Sciences and Policy after a B.Sc.), and 9 in one focus, 6 of them at 400+.

title: Natural Sciences and Technology
points: Only one of each: LSCI 230 or MIMM 211; ENVB 529 or GEOG 201; BREE 217, CIVE 323 or GEOG 322; BIOL 308 or ENVB 305; BIOL 465 or WILD 421; COMP 202 or COMP 204; EPSC 201 or EPSC 233.

title: Faculty of Law
points: Trains jurists across languages, jurisdictions, legal traditions, disciplines and cultures. The double degree compares legal traditions and increasingly includes Indigenous ones, in line with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's calls to action, on Kanien'kehá:ka territory. Teaching is in English and French, in civil and common law, in francophone Montreal.

Professors come from around the world. The 2019 entering class had students born in 29 countries with 15 mother tongues; graduate students come from five continents. The Faculty is working to welcome more kinds of learners, and to better represent Canadian society and Indigenous peoples.

title: Legal Education at McGill
points: Bilingual and pluralistic, so your understanding of law isn't tied to one jurisdiction or tradition.
Integrated first-year coursework in French and English, built on civil and common law, plus Indigenous law and alternate dispute resolution.

Small groups work on legal method, ethics, empirical research and policy. One-week intensives on special topics run in fall and winter. Modern classrooms, with students leading more of their own learning.

title: Location
points: Faculty of Law: Chancellor Day Hall, 3644 Peel St., H3A 1W9, 514-398-6666, mcgill.ca/law.
Undergraduate Admissions: New Chancellor Day Hall, Room 418, 514-398-6602, admissions.law@mcgill.ca.

title: Admissions Policy
points: Reviewers look at the whole application: academic record, languages, motivation, activities and references, plus substantial reading and listening in both English and French. They look for curiosity, engagement, insight, leadership, teamwork, openness, maturity and ethics. No GPA or LSAT cut-offs, and no quotas.
Applications are especially welcome from Indigenous peoples, people with disabilities, racialized people, 2SLGBTQ+ people, women, people from disadvantaged backgrounds, and others facing barriers.

Limited and competitive: about 180 admitted each year, with about eight applicants per place, so many qualified people are refused. The Admissions Office and a committee of professors, senior law students and two Assistant Deans review files.

title: Educational Requirements
points: You need at least 60 university credits, a Quebec DCS, or a Quebec French Baccalaureate (Collège international Marie de France or Collège Stanislas). Not eligible: French Baccalaureate from outside Quebec, IB, or high school students.
Almost everyone admitted as a University applicant has finished a degree. No minimum GPA, LSAT or R-score, though admitted students tend to have outstanding records; the website has statistics.
If you enter from CEGEP or the Quebec Baccalaureate and want to practise in the US, some state bars require university study before law.

title: Language Requirements
points: You must be at least passively bilingual: C1 in one of English or French and B2 reading and listening in the other (CEFR). This is a minimum, not an advantage.

You may write and speak in either language, regardless of the course's language, and do Moot Court in either. First-year courses run in both; some upper-year ones in one only. Exam questions follow the course language but can include long passages in either. Nearly all first-years get at least one French section.

Say how you learned both languages and include language course transcripts, or you'll be refused. Supreme Court of Canada judgments show the reading level expected. If you plan on the Barreau or Chambre des notaires, see the Charter of the French Language requirements (p. 70).

title: Indigenous Applicants
points: First Nations (Status and Non-Status), Inuit, Métis and other Indigenous persons with ties to Turtle Island are encouraged to apply and to self-identify, which helps McGill share services and funding and track recruitment. You may choose another category instead, following its rules.

title: Linguistic Support
points: Don't rule yourself out over language, as English or French may be a third language or feel colonial; talk to the Faculty. The McCarthy Tétrault Fund for Language Training pays for language work before and during the program.

title: Indigenous Student Financial Assistance
points: A McGill funding program, supported in part by Indspire, an Indigenous-led charity.

title: Indigenous Research and Experiential Opportunities
points: Research with scholars in both languages; the Indigenous Law Association; Indigenous Human Rights Initiatives; the Legal Clinic at Kahnawà:ke; L.E.X. with the Kahnawà:ke Survival School; the Kawaskimhon Moot; and a Minor in Indigenous Studies.

Terms away at the University of Arizona's Indigenous Peoples Law and Policy Program or Osgoode Hall's Intensive Program in Indigenous Lands, Resources and Governments. In 2022, a pilot month-long Anishinaabe Law Field School with Manitoba's Treaty Relations Commission. Several funding sources may apply.

title: First Peoples' House
points: A home away from home: community, mentoring, computers, guest lectures, elder visits, academic counselling, a resource centre and housing.

title: Indigenous Law Centre Programming
points: The University of Saskatchewan's centre works on access to legal education, law that better serves Indigenous communities, and sharing information. Incoming Indigenous students are encouraged to look into it first.

title: Honesty and Integrity of Applicants
points: False, incomplete, inconsistent or misleading information is misconduct, whether intended or not. Examples include a personal statement you didn't write, or not disclosing an LSAT score. McGill may refuse you or withdraw an offer, and may report you to LSAC.

title: Application Process for B.C.L./J.D. Degree Program
points: Apply early, with all documents in by the deadline. Only complete files get reviewed.

title: Online Application
points: Online from September 1. Email the Law Admissions Office if you can't apply online (transfer applicants). You should get an acknowledgement within 48 hours; if not, contact them.

title: Verifying the Status of Your Application in the Applicant Portal
points: Watching the Applicant Portal is your job. "Provide supporting documents" means incomplete, and incomplete files are cancelled after the deadline, except when only an LSAT score is missing ("Items outstanding"). "In review" lasts until a decision.

Near deadlines documents can take 48 hours to show up, so contact the office only if your file is still incomplete 48 hours after the deadline. Upload documents through the Portal once you have your acknowledgement.

title: Review of Applications
points: Complete files are assessed against the Admissions Policy and compared with other applicants.

title: Admission Decisions
points: You get an email and the decision in the Portal, never by phone. Review can run into June, and waitlist decisions until the end of August.

title: Application Fee
points: Non-refundable; see Student Accounts for the amount. Requires Visa, MasterCard or American Express, processed through Moneris, and not stored by McGill.

title: Applicant Categories
points: Leading to the degree, September only: University, Mature, CEGEP and Quebec French Baccalaureate, Advanced Standing, Transfer.
Not leading to a degree, September or January: Visiting, Incoming Exchange, Comité des équivalences, Special.

title: University Applicants
points: On track to finish a degree, or with at least 60 undergraduate credits; includes those with over 30 credits beyond a DCS by registration. With 60 credits you may apply, but admission is unlikely unless you'll finish your degree first.

title: Mature Applicants
points: Five or more years away from formal education, not necessarily in a row. You're placed here automatically from your academic history. Same criteria and educational requirements, no set number admitted, and with close attention to professional activities. An interview may be needed.

title: CEGEP and Quebec French Baccalaureate (Collège international Marie de France and Collège Stanislas) Applicants
points: With a DCS or Quebec French Baccalaureate, and up to 30 university credits by registration. Only Collèges Marie de France and Stanislas qualify; a French Baccalaureate or IB from outside Quebec needs 60 full-time university credits first.
Not eligible for joint degrees. Potentially admissible candidates must attend an interview. US practice may require university study before law.

title: Advanced Standing Students
points: For holders of a recognized law degree, typically one allowing a bar exam or graduate law in that jurisdiction, unless using the Comité des équivalences. French applicants need a licence en droit, not a DEUG. Few places; same criteria, with emphasis on your law grades.

Earn at least 75 McGill credits and the integrated B.C.L./J.D.; neither degree stands alone. Usually you take Property, Contractual Obligations and Extra-Contractual Obligations/Torts. The Associate Dean (Academic) sets equivalences.

title: Transfer Students
points: After at least a full-time year at another Canadian law faculty. Few places; same criteria, with emphasis on law grades and your reasons. At least 75 McGill credits, about 2.5 years. Usually you retake the private law courses, with no credit for property, obligations, contracts or torts from your first year.

Send Winter results as soon as you have them; they are needed for evaluation. A law certificate doesn't qualify or count, and you need Good Standing. Online until November 1, deadline May 1; afterwards ask for a paper form.

title: Comité des équivalences
points: For holders of a recognized law degree meeting Barreau du Québec or Chambre des notaires requirements. Submit your equivalency application before the document deadline, and have the final decision by registration. Non-degree, with no credit toward a McGill law degree; not for National Committee on Accreditation requirements.

title: Visiting Students (Letters of Permission)
points: After two years at another law faculty, in Good Standing, spend a term here if space permits. Apply through Admissions with a Letter of Permission. The Director (Student Life and Learning) decides and arranges your courses. Non-degree.

title: Incoming Exchange Students
points: From law programs with a McGill exchange agreement or through BCI. Your home university nominates you and has its own deadlines. Apply online with no fee; generally a B average minimum. The Director decides and it's final. Limited places, with no guarantee of restricted courses. Non-degree.

title: Special Students
points: Exceptional and limited, for compelling academic or professional reasons, if there's space. At most 6 credits a term and 12 in total. Non-degree.

McGill students elsewhere need the Associate Dean's and instructor's permission and use a form. Other Quebec university students apply through BCI. Not for those seeking a law degree, recently refused, or meeting NCA requirements.
Mandatory B.C.L./J.D. courses, 600-level courses and two complementary courses are closed to Special Students.

title: Application Deadlines for Law Undergraduate Programs
points: Online from September 1. Identify your category, since deadlines differ. Late applications are never accepted, and incomplete ones are cancelled the day after the document deadline. Upload everything except references and some transcripts. First-year, Transfer and Advanced Standing start only in September.

title: First Year (Fall)
points: Application / documents: University, November 1 / November 8. Mature, November 1 / November 8. CEGEP and Baccalaureate, March 1 / March 7.

title: Applicants to Upper Years
points: Application / documents, Fall: Advanced Standing, November 1 / January 15. Transfer, May 1 / June 15. Comité des équivalences and Chambre des notaires, May 1 / July 1. Special, August 1 / August 8. Visiting (Fall or Winter), May 1 / June 15. Exchange, April 15 / May 1.
Winter: Exchange, September 15 / October 1. Comité and Chambre, October 1 / December 1. Special, December 1 / December 8.

title: Application Supporting Documents
points: Everyone sends transcripts, a personal statement, a CV and references (not Exchange). Visiting and Exchange add a letter of permission or nomination; Comité applicants the final decision; Exchange a passport copy. LSAT scores come directly from LSAC.
Check your Portal checklist often. With over 1,300 applications a year, logging can take 48 hours near deadlines. Documents become McGill's property and aren't returned or forwarded.

title: Uploading Supporting Documents
points: Upload, don't mail, and don't mail anything already uploaded. Only one version of the personal statement, Extenuating Circumstances form and CV is accepted, so check before uploading. To update transcripts, contact Admissions. Extra items are ignored.

title: Mailing Supporting Documents
points: For documents that can't be uploaded: Law Admissions Office, New Chancellor Day Hall, Room 418, 3644 Peel St., H3A 1W9. Questions: 514-398-6602, admissions.law@mcgill.ca, mcgill.ca/law/bcl-jd.

title: Transcripts
points: A full record of all post-secondary study, updated until a final decision. Quebec universities can send through BCI (ask your registrar), which counts as official. Everything else is uploaded and treated as unofficial until an offer depends on official copies, which come in a sealed envelope or to officialschooldocs@mcgill.ca directly from the school or a service like Parchment.
Scan in the original orientation. McGill may ask for official records at any time and rescind offers over discrepancies.

McGill transcripts are obtained for you, except grades from exchanges. Submit transcripts for exchange, visiting and independent study not on your home transcript. Other languages need a translation by the school or a certified translator.

CEGEP applicants give a Permanent Code, without which processing waits; records come from Quebec from mid-October. Quebec Baccalaureate needs official transcripts. Transfers send Winter results when available. LSDAS and OLSAS aren't used. Report language courses taken outside a degree, with proof.

title: Personal Statement
points: 750 words of your own thinking: why law, why McGill, and what you'd bring. It also shows your writing and judgment in English or French. Members of equity-deserving groups are encouraged to explain how their circumstances and experience relate to studying law here. You don't need to plan on practising.

title: Practical Tips
points: Read the Admissions Policy, think about your motivations, and research law faculties so you can say why McGill. Don't restate your CV; be authentic and original without losing substance.

Write in whichever of English or French you express yourself best, or both; don't use it to prove bilingualism unless you're very comfortable. Check grammar and format, as you get only one submission. Indigenous applicants may add further documents.

title: Format
points: 750 words at most, with the word count at the end. Put your name and McGill ID (from your acknowledgement) at the top right of each page. Re-applicants need a new statement; little change makes you unlikely to be competitive.

title: Extenuating Circumstances
points: If a serious medical or personal difficulty affected your grades for a defined time, file this form. The Admissions Office weighs credibility and documents, dates, and which terms or courses were hit. It may then leave out affected results, at its sole discretion, and its decision is final.

title: Format
points: Declare it in the application; a form then appears on your checklist. Attach at most two pages of supporting documents. One version only; later updates or mailed items aren't added.

title: CV
points: Cover academics, work, volunteering, activities, sports and interests, and languages. It helps show your strength, involvement, leadership and time management.
Give hours worked during your studies and time spent volunteering. Any work counts. Re-applicants must update it.

title: Format
points: Any layout, two pages at most; nothing past that is read. An optional template is on the Admissions Guide's Supporting Documents page.

title: References
points: Exactly two, named in the first two Referee fields; each gets an email with instructions. You may substitute until the document deadline. Indigenous applicants should see their own page.

Students and recent students need professors or teachers who know their work; CEGEP and Quebec Baccalaureate applicants need two college professors. Otherwise use someone who supervises you and can judge reading, research and writing. Personal references don't help, and the office won't chase referees.

title: Requirements
points: Forms must come from an institutional or corporate email, not Hotmail, Gmail, Yahoo, Sympatico or Videotron. Tell referees your category. You're responsible for timely receipt; check your Portal checklist rather than asking the office.

title: Re-applicants
points: Since 2024–2025, name all referees in the Recommendations section, which sends the form. The same people may be used, but they must submit a new one.

title: Law School Admission Test (LSAT)
points: Optional, but any score counts. If you've taken it or will, report dates and your LSAT ID, even if you think it hurts you. Tell Admissions in writing about any later change. Files with pending results wait for review.

title: Consequences of Failure to Disclose
points: Not disclosing the LSAT is material misrepresentation, which can cost you your offer or application at any time. Random checks run during admissions and systematic ones on those offered a place; offers have been revoked before.
Why not required: the test is only in English, which would disadvantage francophone applicants.

Should you take it: with about eight applicants per place, you should apply widely, and almost every law school outside Quebec requires it (except Ottawa's Civil Law and the French Common Law programs at Moncton and Ottawa). Consider it if your grades are below the admitted average GPA of 3.8 (about 85%).
McGill averages multiple sittings. Entering classes average 162: half between 160 and 164, a quarter between 150 and 160, a quarter above 164.
When: by November of the year before entry; results hold up your file. A January sitting risks no places being left. Your status stays "Items outstanding" until the score arrives.

title: Processing of LSAT Results
points: Results come straight from LSAC; reactivate your service if it expired. McGill doesn't run the test; register with LSAC. See the FAQ.

title: Academic Regulations
points: This publication and Faculty Regulations govern Law students for 2026–2027, with any changes published before Fall registration. All may change at any time.

title: Academic Standing
points: A credit system, detailed in the Registration Materials posted at mcgill.ca/law-studies/courses before Minerva opens in May. The Code of Student Conduct also applies.

title: Academic Requirements
points: Finish within five years of first registering unless on approved leave (Reg. 5) or part-time (Reg. 53). You can't also be in a Bar training program (Reg. 4). Full-time means 12+ credits a term, except a final term needing fewer (Reg. 3). No credit for courses counted toward another degree (Reg. 10).
Expect two hours of study per lecture hour, plus essays, seminars and Legal Methodology. No other studies during the session without the Dean's approval.

Evaluation is anonymous (Regs. 19, 22). Write in English or French; exam questions follow the course language but may include either (Reg. 20). If you don't pass a session you must withdraw, but may apply for readmission (Regs. 49, 50).

title: Admission to the Legal Profession
points: The Career Development Office tracks Bar rules for common jurisdictions, but meeting them, including pre-law education, is your job.

title: Admission to the Legal Profession: Canada
points: See each regulator's site. The National Committee on Accreditation, at flsc.ca, handles moves between provincial bars; Comités des équivalences handle transfers to Quebec.

title: Admission to the Legal Profession: The United States
points: The J.D. is approved in some jurisdictions (such as NY and MA), so graduates proceed like US students, with a Foreign Legal Education Evaluation for New York. Some states also need particular pre-law study, so check early; the CDO has information.

title: Overview of Undergraduate Degrees Offered
points: One integrated program gives both the B.C.L. and the J.D. You may add a minor, major or honours, do a joint degree in Management or Social Work, go on exchange, earn non-course or outside credits, or take internships.

title: McGill B.C.L./J.D. Program
points: First-year transsystemic teaching covers both traditions in one course, building analysis and openness. 105 credits, usually in 3.5–4 years, or 3 with summer courses and heavier loads.
You can't combine it with another university program, go part-time to pursue other studies, or take leave for a graduate program.

title: M.B.A./Law Program
points: With Desautels. Apply separately to Law and to the M.B.A.; see mcgill.ca/law-studies/bcljd-studies/joint-MBA.

title: M.S.W./Law Program
points: With the School of Social Work. Apply separately to each; see mcgill.ca/law-studies/bcljd-studies/joint-MSW.

title: Exchange and Study Abroad Options for Law Students
points: About 25% of undergraduates go abroad. McGill students: see the Student Affairs Office. Students from elsewhere: see Incoming Exchange and Visiting Students. General information is on p. 1286.
Credited summer Human Rights Internships run through the Centre for Human Rights and Legal Pluralism; see mcgill.ca/humanrights/clinical/internships and mcgill.ca/cdo.

title: Student Activities and Services
points: Many activities and clubs, mostly under the Law Students Association: lsa-aed.ca.

title: Clinical Legal Education at McGill Law
points: Up to 15 non-course credits for practical learning: human rights internships, court clerkships, mooting, the Legal Clinic Course, law journals, and work as a Legal Methodology Tutorial Leader or Group Assistant.

title: Student Affairs Office
points: New Chancellor Day Hall, Room 433: the Associate Dean (Academic), Assistant Dean (Students), Student Affairs Officer, two Student Advisors and coordinators, helping at every stage.

title: Student Advising and Support
points: Help with stress, productivity, sleep, money or personal problems; drop by or email sao.law@mcgill.ca, and point classmates who struggle here too. Also advice on registration, planning, part-time status, leave, exams, majors, honours, minors, exchanges and summer courses.

title: Academic Accommodations
points: Options include extensions, deferrals, attendance waivers, leave and part-time study. Ask the Student Affairs Office, not your instructors, and bring documents. Student Accessibility and Achievement helps with disabilities and health conditions, temporary or lasting; book through ClockWork.

title: Scholarships and Financial Support
points: The Faculty's awards recognize academics and activities. The Scholarships and Student Aid Office offers aid to full-time degree students: counsellors assess need and guide you to grants, loans, government aid and campus jobs.

title: Student Wellness
points: Workshops in the Academic Success Series, wellness events, and a site on health, money, volunteering, dependents and mentorship. Local Wellness Advisors offer programming, single one-on-one sessions and training for student groups.

title: Law Students' Association/ Association des étudiant.e.s en droit
points: Founded March 12, 1912 and incorporated May 4, 1992, now about 600 members, up from 30. The official Law student body, representing you in the Faculty and beyond and running services and events. Nine elected executives; office in the basement of Old Chancellor Day Hall.

title: Legal Information Clinic at McGill
points: Free, bilingual, student-run legal information, referrals and document certification for McGill and Montreal, with a focus on marginalized groups. Law students past first year can volunteer. SSMU Building, Room 107, 3480 McTavish St.; 514-398-6792; licm.ca.

title: Contours
points: A student magazine since 2012 on women and law, in writing and art. Published yearly in English and French.

title: Graduate Law Student Association
points: Five executives represent all graduate Law students and postdocs at the Faculty and PGSS, sitting on committees and running social and academic events.

title: Innocence McGill
points: Since 2005, a student-run clinic with a supervising lawyer and Faculty Advisor, investigating wrongful conviction claims for serious crimes in Quebec.

title: L.E.X. Program
points: Formerly High School Outreach. Law students and Montreal-area teens learn from each other, responding to dropout rates and the under-representation of underprivileged, immigrant and minority youth.

title: McGill Journal of Law and Health
points: A peer-reviewed, bilingual, student-run journal since 2007 on health law and policy, from medical technology to ethics.

title: McGill Journal of Sustainable Development Law
points: Formerly the International Journal of Sustainable Development Law and Policy. Student-run and peer-reviewed since 2004, connecting law, development, environment, economics and society.

title: McGill Law Journal
points: Student-founded in 1952: critical analysis of public, private and international law, in common and civil law, for professors, lawyers and students.

title: McGill Journal of Dispute Resolution
points: Peer-reviewed since 2014, on domestic and international alternative dispute resolution.

title: Pro Bono Students Canada
points: Founded at Toronto in 1996, now at all 22 Canadian law schools: 1,600 volunteers give about 140,000 free hours to over 400 groups, courts and tribunals yearly. The McGill chapter started in 2000, and in 2012–2013 had 91 volunteers with 32 Montreal organizations.

title: Quid Novi
points: The Faculty's weekly paper, funded by the LSA, with news, satire, poetry and commentary.

title: Skit Nite
points: A yearly student comedy and music show, raising money for Montreal charities.

title: Scholarships, Prizes, and Student Aid for Undergraduate Students
points: The Undergraduate Scholarships and Awards Calendar lists all SSAO aid. Links cover entrance and in-course awards, Law's discretionary prizes, bursaries and loans, and Work Study.

title: Career Development Office
points: Career counselling, led by a lawyer alumnus with a career advisor and Associate: summer jobs, articling and post-graduation options. Employers can post free on myFuture and join on-campus interviews and events.

title: Career Days for Law Students
points: Six a year: career paths, public interest (November, with panels), Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto and US employers.

title: On-Campus Recruitment for the Faculty of Law
points: On-campus interviews: US (August), Vancouver and Calgary (September), Toronto (October), Ottawa (January), with processes for other cities. Montreal's Course aux stages happens at firms' offices, with step-by-step CDO help.

title: Resource Centre of the Faculty of Law CDO
points: Publications on job searches, diversity and employers, a website, and the myFuture job tool.

title: Faculty of Law Training Programs and Publications
points: Seminars, one-on-one counselling, newsletters for each recruitment process, mock interviews, guides, and panels and networking with alumni.

title: About the Desautels Faculty of Management
points: A very international business school with students and professors from every continent and a focus on global issues. Internships and exchanges in Europe, Asia, the US and South America.

title: About the Bachelor of Commerce (BCom)Program
points: Prepares you for professional and managerial careers through critical thinking, integrating disciplines, applying theory, teamwork and leadership. A broad core gives quantitative, analytical and communication skills; specializations add depth.

General Management: focus on at least two areas, one Management concentration plus a second concentration or an outside minor. Suits a broad business education, later study such as law or industrial relations, or careers across sectors.
Majors and honours focus on one area, for clear goals or designations such as CPA or CFA.

International Management: the International Business Concentration, an outside Minor, a language to intermediate level, and international learning through exchange, study away or a study trip; credits vary by courses taken abroad.
Honours in Investment Management combines rigorous study with real investing, global internships and corporate partners.

title: Administrative Officers
points: Yolande Chan, Dean. Benjamin Croitoru, Associate Dean, Undergraduate Programs. Heather McCombie, Associate Director, BCom Program. Jennifer Hunter, Associate Director, Student Affairs.

title: B.Com. Degree Requirements
points: 120 credits full-time over three or four years; generally 90 with Advanced Standing or a Quebec CEGEP diploma. Those from outside Quebec without an equivalent need 120.
Everyone needs a 3-credit experiential learning course. Teaching is in English, but you may submit work and write exams in French, which matters for business in Quebec.

title: Absence Policy
points: Attend regularly and tell your instructor promptly about absences and why. No documents needed for illness under five days. A medical note may be requested after five consecutive days if you miss a required activity or assessment. Missing over 20% of a course may be impossible to accommodate; withdrawal may be best. For repeated trouble contact bcom.mgmt@mcgill.ca.

Non-medical absences like varsity events may need documents. You make up missed learning. For a missed assessment with a valid reason, ask your instructor, who follows PASL article 7 and judges what's fair and workable. Instructors are encouraged to plan flexible assessments.

title: Academic Advising
points: The BCom Student Affairs Office advises all year on your degree, courses and policies, but you lead your own planning and are responsible for meeting requirements and deadlines.

Review your unofficial transcript and myProgress regularly, though myProgress can make mistakes, so check against the catalogue and Areas of Study page. Verify registration before add/drop ends. A graduation check before your final term is required.

Math and Statistics or Economics majors also see a departmental advisor. Minors need departmental advising and an approval form signed for the BCom office. Career Coaches are on the 6th floor of Bronfman.

title: When to Contact an Academic Advisor
points: For requirements, planning, registration, myProgress questions, changing programs, exams, summer courses, transfer credits, exchange, IUT, internships, leave, personal difficulties, long absences, policies, Academic Standing, the experiential requirement, and graduation.
They also help students elsewhere in Joint Honours Economics or the Minors in Management and Entrepreneurship, and prospective students; admissions questions go to Service Point.
See the BCom office site, the catalogue, or the BCom Hub in myCourses. Appointments in person or virtual through BCom Insight. A Local Wellness Advisor and the Wellness Hub also help.
Every new student must meet an advisor between October and the end of the first term, by email or booking form.

title: Academic Requirements for Graduation
points: Staff advise, but you are fully responsible for course choices, requirements, rules and deadlines. Misunderstanding won't earn an exception.
120 credits; a Quebec CEGEP diploma gives 30 of Advanced Standing, for 90. Others without an equivalent need 120. New students should verify transfer credits with an advisor.

title: Students Entering with Advanced Standing
points: Meet an advisor and get official results in by the end of your first term, or the credit may be denied. Deviating from your program needs the Associate Director's written permission. Transfers from other universities need at least 60 credits in the BCom.

title: Experiential Learning Degree Requirement
points: At least 3 credits for those admitted from Fall 2024. Majors in Business Analytics, Managing for Sustainability or Retail Management and Honours in Investment Management can meet it through their program; check the course repository. Others use an elective or complementary. Not all run each term, so plan ahead.

title: Academic Standing
points: Based mainly on CGPA, and sometimes TGPA. Assessed in January for Fall, May for Winter, and September for Summer; it decides if and how you continue. Fall results are "Interim", since deferred exams and two-term courses aren't counted yet. If not Satisfactory, see an advisor before withdrawal deadlines.

title: Satisfactory/Interim Satisfactory Standing
points: CGPA of 2.00 or more; new students start here. You continue, and you need a 2.00 CGPA to graduate.

title: Probationary/Interim Probationary Standing
points: You continue at a maximum of 14 credits a term, raise your GPA, and must see an advisor. Interim Probationary: review your load and strongly consider advice before Winter.

From Satisfactory: CGPA 1.50–1.99. Staying on Probation: CGPA 1.50–1.99 and TGPA 2.50+ (no TGPA test for Summer). From Interim Unsatisfactory: same CGPA and TGPA. Readmitted from Unsatisfactory: CGPA under 2.00, and meet your letter's conditions.

title: Unsatisfactory Readmitted Standing
points: Applies after being readmitted from Unsatisfactory. Your letter sets your load and conditions; see an advisor.

title: Unsatisfactory/Interim Unsatisfactory Standing
points: Interim: you may continue but must see an advisor before Winter withdrawal deadlines. Unsatisfactory: you can't continue, and your registration is cancelled.
Appeal in Minerva by July 15 (Fall) or November 15 (Winter), with proof of extenuating circumstances and reassurance of improvement. A second time means permanent withdrawal.
Triggers: CGPA below 1.50; or, from Probationary, Unsatisfactory Readmitted or Interim Unsatisfactory, TGPA below 2.50 with CGPA below 2.00.

title: Incomplete Standings
points: Standing awaits deferred exam, or Standing Incomplete. From Winter or Summer you may register for Fall, but it must be resolved by add/drop's end. Unsatisfactory then cancels registration; see your advisor at once, as readmission needs proof and reassurance.

title: Transfer Credit and Advanced Standing
points: Up to 30 credits of Advanced Standing for good results in the DCS, IB, French or European Baccalaureate, Bologna countries, A and AS Levels, or AP. Transfers may cover up to a third of your degree, including program requirements.

See p. 55 for grades. P or S transfer only from McGill faculties. Letter grades from the other school take precedence. Get approval before exchange or study away. Residency: 80 credits for four-year, 60 for three-year. At most 6 online credits with department approval.

title: Course Overlap
points: No credit for content overlapping McGill, CEGEP or other university courses, AP, A Levels, IB or French Baccalaureate. Ask the office and read exclusions.

Statistics: use the courses in Core and your program; others are judged case by case. Take them in order: MGCR 271 and MGSC 372 before MATH 324, never after. MATH 203, 204, PSYC 204 and 305 aren't open. Transferring from another faculty, McGill's MATH 203 exempts MGCR 271, but a pre-McGill MATH 203 doesn't.
Economics: at most 6 credits of Foundation courses; 9 among ECON 230D1/D2, 250D1/D2 and MGCR 293; 9 among ECON 332, 333, 295 and MGCR 294. ECON 208 and 209 aren't allowed; ECON 230D1/D2 isn't for U0.
The BCom is full-time, with part-time only for an occasional term in unusual circumstances.

title: Course Requirements
points: C or better in all required and complementary courses, including Foundation. Repeat a failed required course, normally once; failure means below C, or J or KF. Substitutions only in special cases.

A failed complementary can be repeated or replaced; a replaced D stays as an elective credit. A repeated required D gives credit once. Both Ds count in your CGPA. Repeating a course you passed with C or better earns no credit and no CGPA effect.

title: Courses Taken Under the Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory Option
points: Electives only, one per term, up to 10% of your McGill credits, chosen or cancelled by add/drop's end. S/U isn't in your GPA. Scholarships require 27 graded credits a year excluding Summer, so ask before using it. See p. 36.

title: Cumulative Grade Point Average (CGPA)
points: Graduate after your minimum credits and curriculum with a CGPA of 2.00, or 3.00 for Honours.

title: Non-Management Electives
points: Taking electives outside Desautels is strongly encouraged; Arts and Science are typically fine. Check eligibility in Minerva and the Restricted Electives page before add/drop ends. 100–200 level is suggested. Desautels courses can also serve.
Some faculties won't block you despite missing prerequisites, so check. Some departments such as Psychology reserve seats, so open spots may not be available.

Categories, subject to availability: AFRI, ANTH, ARTH, ATOC, BIOL, CANS, CATH, CHEM, CLAS, COMS, COMP, EAST, EPSC, ECON, ED (restricted), ENGL, ENVR, FREN, FRSL, GSFS, GEOG, HIST, INDG, INTD, ISLA, JWST, GERM, HISP, ITAL, LLCU, RUSS, LING, MATH, MUAR, MUTH, MUPD, MUHL (restricted), PHIL, PHYS, POLI, PSYC, PPOL, QCST, RELG, SOCI, WCOM (restricted).

title: Registration
points: Register on time; space is limited. Returning students' priority for Fall and Winter starts in the last week of May; Summer Management courses open in early March.

If you can't get a course you need, send a Closed Course Request Form right after registering; waiting until add/drop can delay graduation. Continuing Studies courses don't count. Check credit and overlaps yourself: being let in by Minerva doesn't guarantee credit.
New students pick their specialization in Minerva first or get blocked; this can change later. Major and Concentration Fair for U1 each March. Watch BCom Hub alerts.

Changes in add/drop go through Minerva. Later withdrawals before the deadline give a W, with no GPA effect; after it, only in exceptional cases, starting with an advisor, and with substantial documents. Courses breaking rules get flagged not for credit.

New students: most decisions come by end of May, with registration in early to mid-June. Attend a virtual session in early June and in-person orientation. Advising runs May to classes by booking form. Use your McGill email from the moment you accept.

title: Advising Schedules
points: Drop-in during add/drop and peak times for registration topics. 30-minute appointments after add/drop. An information session is required before exchange advising.

title: Time and Credit Limit for Completion of the B.Com. Degree
points: With 90 or fewer credits to do, finish within eight terms of first registering; with over 90, this applies from a year after first registering. After a year or more away, request readmission in Minerva and in writing to bcom.mgmt@mcgill.ca; current requirements usually apply.

title: BCom Degree Admission Requirements
points: Highly selective, and minimums don't guarantee a place. See the admissions guide. Those required to withdraw elsewhere for poor grades can't transfer in. The office has interfaculty transfer details.

title: Location
points: Samuel Bronfman Building, Room 228, 1001 Sherbrooke St. W., H3A 1G5; 514-398-4068; bcom.mgmt@mcgill.ca.

title: About BCom Student Affairs Office
points: Advice on programs, requirements, registration, withdrawals, exams, rereads, Academic Standing, transfers, exchanges, scholarships, graduation and experiential learning, plus help through personal, financial or medical trouble. Immigration questions go to International Student Services or Service Point. Book through BCom Insight, or visit Room 228 if you can't.

title: Grading and Credit
points: In week one each instructor gives a written outline with topics, readings, office hours and contact details.

title: Policy on Assessment of Student Learning
points: From PASL. The outline lists each assessment's due date, weight, structure, late penalties and delivery. Optional alternatives must be clear and open to all. If assessment changes after add/drop, you can choose original or new by a set date.

All due before the last exam day. No in-term tasks due in the last 10 working days of classes, except language orals, take-homes given at least 15 working days before classes end, and tasks worth 10% or less.

title: Academic Integrity
points: Know what counts as cheating and plagiarism under the Code. New undergraduates complete the Academic Integrity tutorial in Minerva.

title: Honours and First-Class Honours
points: Honours: CGPA and program GPA of 3.0+. First-Class: both 3.5+. If below 3.0 or missing requirements, ask your advisor about graduating in another program.

title: Dean's Honour List and Distinction
points: See Graduation Honours (p. 67).

points: Merit-only awards are automatic for Fall or Winter graduates before Spring Convocation.

Apply online by early May: Anil Gondi Community Impact Award; B.Com. Class of 1986 Activity Award for Leadership; B.Com. Class of 1990 Activity Award; Jaclyn Lea Fisher Volunteer Leadership Award; Richard G. Donovan Prize in Case Excellence; Stephen S. Goldbloom Memorial Prize.

title: In-Course Scholarships, Prizes, and Awards
points: Requires 27 graded credits in fall and winter, or 14 in one term. Merit-only awards are automatic; those mixing academics, volunteering and leadership need one online application by early June.

Application needed: Commerce 1955, Danny and Monica Gold, Devon Anthony Haye, Donald R. McRobie, Dr. Alex Paterson, Great-West Life and London Life, Hazelview, HSBC, Marcel A. Desautels, Marion McCall Daly, Paul-Hervé Desrosiers, Peter Brojde, Sheila Wellington BMO, Shirin Yeganegi, Anil Gondi (every three years), Philippe and Nan-B de Gaspé Beaubien (odd years).

Automatic: Accenture, André Desmarais and Francine Chrétien-Desmarais, Barry Clamen, Cecil Vineberg, Commerce 1953, Deloitte, Dorothy Esmé Graham Snell, Elizabeth Macfarlane, Frederick M. Connell, Gary and Wendy Balter, George Arnold Hart, Gerald Benjamin Wasserman, Jon Hartwick, John V. Galley, Joseph H. Jacobs, Letko Brosseau, McGill Alumnae Helen R. Y. Reid, Richter, Robert Bruce, Sir William Macdonald, Sujata Madan, Women Associates of McGill. The Dobson Centre awards the Dobson Cup Grit Prize and Peter Johnson Start-Up Prize.

You must be full-time in the BCom the next fall and winter, or full-time at McGill while not on exchange. Summer or Fall graduates can't get these but can apply for graduating awards. Awards are revoked if you stop qualifying, and aren't kept while you're on leave.

title: Examinations
points: See p. 62. Enrolment Services posts schedules around early November and March and seating late in the last week of classes, and emails you about conflicts. Don't book travel before the schedule is out. A D or F means retaking core and program courses, though D passes for electives.

title: Supplemental Examinations
points: None in undergraduate Desautels courses. To improve, repeat the course in a later term; extra work isn't allowed.

title: Deferred Examinations
points: Never arrange a makeup with your professor. If illness or another serious reason stops you, apply in Minerva; documents may be needed, dated within 5 days of the exam, sent to the office quickly. If approved, write in the official period: March for Fall, August for Winter and Summer. Check the schedule yourself and see an advisor.

title: Verification of Grades and Rereads
points: Under the Charter you may see any marked work and discuss it. If you suspect a final grade error, submit a Re-Read Application Form; during term, go to the instructor first.
Two types: coursework and final exams. Reviewers judge whether the original grade was fair, not regrade from scratch. A new grade replaces the old, higher or lower.

title: Reread of Coursework
points: Apply within 10 working days of getting work back; it's usually done within 20. Group work needs everyone's consent, with one fee. Talk to the instructor first.

title: Rereads of Final Exams
points: Apply in writing by March 31 for Fall and September 30 for Winter or Summer, strictly. Talking to the instructor is recommended. Courses from other faculties follow those faculties' rules.

title: International Exchange Program
points: Over 60 business schools worldwide. Requires a CGPA of 3.0, and at least two-thirds of departmental requirements done at McGill.

After nomination, check courses in the Course Equivalency Database and get transfer approval for all courses, electives included, with the TCAF in Minerva before classes start abroad. Letter grades only, no pass-fail; no credit for overlaps. Outside-program courses need departmental approval. Complete the Travel Registry or risk cancellation, and have your final transcript sent. Questions: 514-398-4068, bcom.mgmt@mcgill.ca.

points: For those who want to understand and use financial information, not become accountants. Part of General Management, with courses serving other programs too.

points: Practical data analysis methods and tools across management fields.

title: Program Description
points: Starting and managing new ventures, including social enterprises and co-ops, with a major field project and courses from across the Faculty.

title: Program Description
points: Ethics issues in management: social responsibility, transparency, compliance, product safety, data use, UN Sustainable Development Goals, and fair labour.

title: Program Description
points: Finance theory, institutions, investment analysis and risk. Leads to careers in finance, government and other firms, up to roles like Treasurer or V.P. Finance.

title: Program Description
points: How organizations use IT: the digital economy, choosing and applying technology, and handling data.

title: Program Description
points: Skills for sound management policy across borders. Prepares you for trade, multinationals, banks and government.

title: Program Description
points: Employer-employee relations and HR, at the personal level and in their wider context. For more depth, consider the Major.

title: Program Description
points: Skills for policies that support sustainable, responsible development: linked economic, social and ecological challenges, sustainability in business functions, and leading change.

title: Complementary Courses (9 credits)
points: 3–9 and 0–6 from two lists, or a related topics course approved by the Mentor and BCom Office.

title: Program Description
points: Theory and practice for jobs in product management, advertising, sales, pricing, research, distribution and retail.

title: Program Description
points: Designing and improving processes that make products and services, using quantitative and cross-functional thinking. Careers in consulting, manufacturing, retail, transport, health care and government.

title: Program Description
points: Behaviour at work, preparing you for graduate study, general management or HR.

title: Program Description
points: Business basics plus hands-on work in the Retail Innovation Lab: running retail at every level with current technology, consumer behaviour, omni-channel, pricing analytics, payments and global value chains.

title: Program Description
points: One of two Strategic Management options. Business in a global setting and its effects on society and the environment: industry structure, competition, organizational capabilities, and different economic and political systems. Leads to consulting, strategic planning in multinationals and government, and business development in start-ups.

title: Program Description
points: Using non-profit, civil and for-profit sectors to tackle social issues. Rethinks strategy around development, environment, responsibility and impact, with cross-sector work and social entrepreneurship, and courses outside the Faculty encouraged. Leads to NGOs, UN-linked bodies, social enterprise, government, consulting and CSR.

title: Minors for Management Students
points: Arts and Science minors work with any B.Com. unless a department says otherwise; ask a departmental advisor first. Check requirements in a Minerva Degree Evaluation, and return a Minor Approval Form signed by the minor advisor to the office, or the minor may not be granted.
Economics: 18 credits not overlapping Management content, with at most 6 for MGCR 293 and ECON 230D1/D2 or 250D1/D2, and 6 for MGCR 294 or ECON 332 and 333. BCom Office approval needed.
Math, Statistics or Computer Science minors: take MATH 133, 140 and 141 and ask the department.

title: McGill University Designated Teaching Hospitals
points: Teaching hospitals are closely tied to McGill and form its clinical departments.

McGill University Health Centre (MUHC): merged teaching hospitals giving advanced bilingual adult and pediatric care. Yearly: 519,000+ ambulatory visits, 32,600+ inpatients, 29,600+ surgeries, 2,800+ births. Sites: Glen (1001 Decarie Blvd.: Children's, Royal Victoria, Chest Institute, Cedars Cancer Centre); Montreal General (1650 Cedar Ave.); The Neuro (3801 University St.); Lachine Hospital (650 16th Ave.); CHSLD Camille-Lefebvre (637, 13e Ave.); Reproductive Centre (888 de Maisonneuve E., Suite 200); Adult Ophthalmology Clinic (5252 de Maisonneuve W.).

17,000+ people across seven missions: Medicine, Surgery, Neurosciences, Mental Health, Women's Health, Cancer Care, Children's. In 2024–2025: 3,793 nursing and related staff, 2,098 other health professionals, 3,493 research members, 1,414 physicians, 150 pharmacists, 339 managers, 2,237 office staff, 2,531 paratechnical and trades, 863 volunteers. Every physician is a McGill professor. It trains 5,200+ a year: 1,000+ residents, 2,500 nursing, 980 medical and 700 others.

Research Institute of the MUHC: 744 researchers, 1,490+ trainees and 1,476 staff, at Glen and the General, partly FRQS funded; rimuhc.ca. The MUHC is also the server lab for Montreal's OPTILAB cluster.

Jewish General Hospital (CIUSSS West-Central, 3755 Côte Ste-Catherine Rd.): since 1934, 637 beds. Yearly 22,000+ admissions, about 592,000 outpatient and 92,000+ emergency visits, 3,600+ births, 12,000+ surgeries. Known for oncology (Segal Cancer Centre), cardiology, neonatology, orthopedics, family medicine, aging and emergency. A Quebec centre for high-risk obstetrics and breast referral, and an early COVID-19 hospital. About 850 doctors and 300+ residents. Hosts McGill's Wainberg Centre for Viral Diseases and translational cancer, head and neck, and menopause programs. Its Lady Davis Institute leads in cancer, aging, epidemiology, nursing, cardiovascular, genetics and more.

St. Mary's Hospital Center (CIUSSS West Island, 3830 Lacombe Ave.): 271 adult beds, university-affiliated. In 2024–2025, 3,551+ births; first Montreal hospital with WHO Baby Friendly recognition. Family medicine, dialysis, oncology, geriatrics, imaging. Yearly 104,509+ clinic visits, 7,113 day surgeries, 14,489+ admissions. Its Research Centre covers cancer, surgery, older adults and primary care.

Douglas Mental Health University Institute (CIUSSS West Island, 6875 LaSalle Blvd.): founded in 1881, WHO-affiliated, for child, adult and geriatric care with a focus on rehabilitation and community. 134,589+ interventions yearly. One of Canada's largest mental health research centres, with 64 scientists and 450+ students in 2024–2025, and McGill centres on schizophrenia, aging and suicide, plus a PAHO/WHO Collaborating Centre.

points: Instruction is in English, but most Québec clinical placements need English and French, so build skills early.

title: Proof of Proficiency in French

title: Vaccination/Immunization Requirements for Health Sciences Programs
points: Compulsory: begin once accepted, finish well before patient contact, with proof signed by a nurse or physician. No exceptions; otherwise you're asked to withdraw. Influenza and others may be required.
D.M.D., General Practice Residency and Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery applicants are tested for Hepatitis B. A positive "e" antigen or viral DNA result withdraws the offer.

Students seropositive for Hepatitis B, C, HIV or other blood-borne pathogens must tell the Dean or Director, and follow the provincial service's recommendations, which may restrict procedures and could mean withdrawing. Those who know they carry such pathogens should weigh this carefully.
With a contagious disease that risks patients, tell your supervisor; you may have to pause clinical work.

Medicine and Dentistry have further UGME policies, and Nursing its own list. Physical and Occupational Therapy need complete records and a mask fitting before the first clinical course, with a card submitted by the third clinical seminar.

title: About the Department of Pharmacology and Therapeutics
points: How the main drug classes act, what modifies their effects, and how drugs are chosen.

title: Other Courses
points: Courses on where and how drugs act, from body to molecule, for its undergraduate students, plus M.Sc. and Ph.D. See p. 1245.

title: About the Department of Physiology
points: Builds on biology, chemistry, math and physics and overlaps other biomedical sciences, feeding clinical medicine. Studies molecules to whole systems in vertebrates: biomathematics, biophysics, cardiovascular, endocrine, gastrointestinal and renal, immunology, neurophysiology, exercise and respiratory. M.Sc., Ph.D. and the M.D.,C.M. & Ph.D. See p. 1266.

title: About The Goodman Cancer Institute
points: Hands-on training for cancer researchers. Investigators belong to eight departments, including Biochemistry, Biomedical Engineering, Human Genetics, Medicine (Experimental), Microbiology and Immunology, and Physiology. Graduate students apply to a program and pick a Full Member as supervisor. Offers labs, technology platforms, mentors, events and internal funding.

title: About The Victor Phillip Dahdaleh Institute of Genomic Medicine
points: Brings genomics into clinical care with the Faculty and MUHC, focused on cancer, neuroscience and mental health, chronic inflammation and infection. Combines genomic and clinical data for diagnosis, targeted therapy and personalized medicine. A joint Ph.D. with Kyoto University. A social sciences pillar studies ethics, law and policy.

title: Core Medical Courses
points: Contributes to FMD and TCP. See Elective Courses.

title: Introduction to Epidemiology and Biostatistics
points: Lectures and tutorials on research design, bias, screening, statistics and reading the literature critically.

title: Clinical Electives in Public Health and Preventive Medicine ( DSP de Montréal)
points: Rotations at Montreal's public health department, in communicable disease or environmental health (on-call, surveillance, investigations) or prevention and promotion (childhood, youth, chronic disease, inequality).

title: Postgraduate Medical Education (Residency in Public Health and Preventive Medicine)
points: Trains specialists to find population health problems and to plan and evaluate programs, drawing on epidemiology, statistics, administration and economics.

title: Graduate Courses in Epidemiology
points: Not currently accepting M.Sc. (Non-Thesis) applications. Offered since the 1960s, strongly quantitative. Strengths: biostatistics, informatics, environmental and occupational health, health care delivery, infectious disease, pharmacoepidemiology, public health, social and reproductive epidemiology, methods, chronic disease, global health, causal inference. M.Sc. (Thesis), M.Sc. (Non-Thesis), Ph.D.

title: Graduate Courses in Biostatistics
points: Statistics for biomedicine, with one of Canada's largest medical school groups of Ph.D. statisticians, funded by NSERC and others, developing new methods. M.Sc. (Thesis), M.Sc. (Non-Thesis), Ph.D.

title: Graduate Courses in Public Health (M.Sc.P.H.)
points: Trains public health professionals and leaders in methods, research and practice, with epidemiology and biostatistics for designing and analyzing studies.

title: Graduate Courses in Occupational Health
points: Ph.D. and M.Sc.A. (Distance and Resident) aren't accepting applications. Multidisciplinary work on dust, chemical and radiation hazards. Applied programs train practitioners and hygienists, with a part-time distance option; research programs train independent researchers.

title: About the Department of Equity, Ethics, and Policy
points: Created in 2021 from the Institute of Health and Social Policy and the Biomedical Ethics Unit. Research, teaching and outreach on how policy is made and how policy and social conditions affect health, with government and community partners.

title: Graduate Program
points: A Master's specialization in Bioethics: courses, a practicum and a thesis. You graduate with an M.A., M.Sc. or LL.M. in your base discipline, from Law, Medicine and Health Sciences, Religious Studies or Philosophy.

title: About the Department of Global and Public Health
points: Tackles health inequities through action-oriented research, interdisciplinary training and equitable partnerships. Faculty focus on solving complex problems; students learn on real problems with stakeholders and communities.

title: Undergraduate Studies with the Department of Global and Public Health
points: Global and Public Health offers the Faculty Program in Population and Global Health (B.A.), p. 386.

title: School of Population and Global Health

See Minerva for all summer courses.

title: Annual Summer Session in Epidemiology and Biostatistics: June 1 to June 26, 2026
points: One-, two- or four-week courses for health professionals, related fields and scientists; graduate students can earn credit faster. Taught in English; work may be in English or French. Credit for graduate students and McGill residents and fellows, through Minerva. Other Quebec students use BCI; other Canadian students use the Graduate Transfer Agreement; others get a Professional Interest Certificate. Fees vary. 2001 McGill College Ave., Suite 1200.
